The policy must prevent convenience-based or excessive collection through interfaces.
All APIs, files, events and data requests collecting participant, provider, plan, payment or review data.
Every integration must document its NDIS purpose and collect only the minimum data needed for that purpose.

Protected Agency information may only be used or disclosed as authorised; unauthorised use or disclosure is prohibited.
Integrations are disclosure mechanisms and need controls equivalent to statutory secrecy controls.
Internal, partner, provider and government integrations handling protected Agency information.
Protected Agency information must not be sent, exposed, cached, transformed or reused unless the disclosure is authorised and logged.

NDIS Act 2013, ss 66-67; Protection and Disclosure of Information Rules 2013
Disclosure of protected information requires an approved pathway, delegate authority or permitted rule.
Outbound integrations must not rely on connectivity alone as proof of lawful release.
Outbound data flows to providers, agencies, partners, researchers and other authorised recipients.
Outbound integrations must identify the approved disclosure authority before production access is granted.
National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013 and related NDIS Rules

Communications and notices should support accessible formats for people with disability.
Integration-generated messages can affect participant rights and access to Scheme services.
Participant-facing notices, portal messages, consent flows and provider/partner messages that trigger participant action.
Participant-facing information produced by integrations must be accessible and easy to understand.

Statutory purpose and lawful information exchange
The NDIS Act establishes the Scheme, the NDIA and the governance arrangements for Scheme administration.
The integration policy must support statutory functions and Scheme integrity, not generic technology exchange only.
All NDIA integration patterns and lifecycle controls.
Integrations must enable secure, reliable and reusable exchange only where they support NDIA functions, participant outcomes and Scheme integrity.
National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013 and related NDIS Rules

Governance, risk ownership and shared accountability
The Accountable Authority determines their entity's tolerance for security risks and documents in the security plan.
Integration risk decisions must be traceable to an approved security risk tolerance so reusable patterns and exceptions do not exceed NDIA's acceptable risk position.
Direct. Applies to all NDIA integrations, especially those exchanging participant, provider, partner or other government data.
Governance, accountability and integration risk management

Integration designs must be assessed against NDIA's security risk tolerance and recorded in the security plan or security risk register. Residual risks above tolerance must be escalated to the accountable authority or delegate before implementation.
Governance, risk ownership and shared accountability
A risk steward (or manager) is identified for each security risk or category of security risk, including shared risks.
Integrations create shared risks across systems, providers and partners; each risk needs a named steward to prevent gaps in ownership and treatment.
Direct. Applies to NDIA-owned systems, shared integration platforms, partner connections and provider-managed services.
Roles, responsibilities and shared risk ownership

Every integration must have named business, system and security risk owners. Shared risks across NDIA, partner, provider or government systems must have a nominated risk steward and documented treatment ownership.
Governance, risk ownership and shared accountability
The Accountable Authority considers the impact that their security risk management decisions could potentially have on other entities, and shares information on risks where appropriate.
Integration risk decisions can affect other entities that consume or provide data; the policy needs a mechanism for considering and communicating those impacts.
Direct. Relevant where NDIA connects to partner, provider, state, territory, Commonwealth or whole-of-government services.
Shared risk assessment and inter-entity notification

NDIA must assess downstream impacts on integrated entities before approving integration patterns, control exceptions or risk acceptances and must share relevant risk information with affected entities through agreed governance channels.
Supplier, procurement, contract and assurance controls

The entity is accountable for the management of security risks arising from procuring goods and services and ensures procurement and contract decisions do not expose the entity or the Australian Government to an unacceptable level of risk.
Third-party integration products and services can expose NDIA and government data to supplier, connectivity and service-chain risks; these must be assessed before procurement or onboarding.
Direct. Applies to integration platforms, API gateways, managed services, SaaS connectors, middleware, data exchange services and support providers.
Third-party and partner integration risk management

Procurement and onboarding of integration products, platforms and providers must include a security risk assessment before engagement and must not expose NDIA or Australian Government systems, information or resources to unacceptable risk.
Supplier, procurement, contract and assurance controls

Procurement, contracts and third-party outsourced arrangements contain proportionate security terms and conditions to ensure service providers, contractors and subcontractors comply with relevant PSPF Requirements.
Contracted integration services must contain enforceable security obligations so PSPF and NDIA controls remain effective beyond NDIA-operated systems.
Direct. Applies to all contracts and outsourcing arrangements that design, build, host, operate, support or connect to NDIA integrations.

Contracts and integration agreements must contain proportionate security requirements for identity and access, encryption, logging, incident reporting, vulnerability management, data handling, subcontracting and compliance with applicable PSPF, ISM and NDIA controls.
Supplier, procurement, contract and assurance controls
Entity ensures service providers, contractors and subcontractors comply with relevant PSPF Requirements as detailed by the entity.
Service-provider compliance must be mandated because integration security depends on provider and subcontractor control implementation.
Direct. Applies to vendors, contractors, subcontractors, delivery partners and managed service providers supporting NDIA integrations.
Service providers, contractors and subcontractors supporting integrations must implement NDIA-specified PSPF, ISM and NDIA security controls and provide evidence of compliance on request.
Incident response, breach notification and cyber/crisis reporting

Contractual security terms and conditions require service providers to report any actual or suspected security incidents to the entity, and follow reasonable direction from the entity arising from incident investigations.
Integration incidents may compromise exchanged data or connected systems; timely provider reporting and cooperation must be contractually required.
Direct. Applies to all third-party and partner integrations, including API, file transfer, messaging, event, data replication and support channels.

Contracts and integration agreements must require providers to notify NDIA of actual or suspected security incidents affecting integrations or exchanged data within agreed timeframes and to follow NDIA incident investigation, containment and recovery directions.
Supplier, procurement, contract and assurance controls
Government entities providing outsourced services provide IRAP assessment reports to the government entities consuming, or looking to consume, their services.
Where NDIA consumes outsourced services from another government entity or shared platform, independent assurance reports are required to support integration authorisation.
Conditional direct. Applies when NDIA consumes outsourced ICT services, shared government services or government-provided integration platforms.
Assurance evidence for shared government services

Where NDIA consumes outsourced ICT services from another government entity or shared platform, integration onboarding must obtain and review current IRAP assessment reports or equivalent assurance before use and upon material change.
Supplier, procurement, contract and assurance controls

Contract security terms and conditions are monitored and reviewed to ensure the specified security controls, terms and conditions are implemented, operated and maintained by the contracted provider, including any subcontractors, over the life of a contract.
Security terms are only effective if monitored over the contract life, including subcontractors and changes to integration services.
Direct. Applies to integration providers and support contracts throughout planning, onboarding, operation, change and exit.

Security terms for integration services must be monitored over the life of the contract, including subcontractor controls, with periodic evidence reviews, assurance activities and treatment tracking for identified gaps.
Supplier, procurement, contract and assurance controls
Contractual terms and conditions include appropriate security arrangements for the completion or termination of the contract.
Integration exit controls are needed to prevent residual access, orphaned credentials, unmanaged data copies and unsupported interfaces after contract completion or termination.
Direct. Applies to all partner, provider and outsourced integration arrangements.
Integration offboarding, termination and exit controls

Integration contracts must specify completion and termination controls, including disabling accounts, revoking credentials and certificates, removing network routes, returning or destroying data, decommissioning interfaces, retaining required logs and confirming that partner or provider access has ceased.
Supplier, procurement, contract and assurance controls
Procurement and contract decisions consider the security risks before engaging providers operating under foreign ownership, control or influence.
Foreign ownership, control or influence can affect data sovereignty, support access, jurisdiction, lawful access and supply-chain risk for integrations.
Direct. Applies to integration procurements, cloud or managed services, SaaS connectors, APIs and providers with offshore ownership, hosting, support or subcontracting.
Foreign ownership, control and influence assessment

Integration procurements must consider foreign ownership, control or influence of providers and service chains before approval and must document mitigations for data sovereignty, privileged support access, jurisdiction, subcontracting and continuity risks.
Supplier, procurement, contract and assurance controls
Security risks arising from contractual arrangements for the provision of goods and services are managed, reassessed and adjusted over the life of a contract.
Third-party integration risks change over time due to contract, architecture, threat, subcontractor and control changes; lifecycle reassessment is mandatory.
Direct. Applies to all third-party and outsourced integrations while they remain connected to NDIA systems or data.

Third-party integration risks must be reassessed during onboarding, renewal, major change, incident response, threat changes and contract review, and controls or access must be adjusted to maintain an acceptable residual risk position.
Supplier, procurement, contract and assurance controls
Secure and verifiable third-party vendors, providers, partners and associated services are used unless business operations require use, and the residual risks are managed and approved by the CISO.
Secure and verifiable vendors and endpoints reduce the risk of integrating with untrusted services, unsupported libraries or unmanaged partner systems.
Direct. Applies to integration platforms, API products, connectors, gateways, libraries, managed services, partner endpoints and provider services.
Approved vendors, products and integration services

Only secure, verifiable vendors, APIs, libraries, managed services and partner endpoints may be used for NDIA integrations unless a business exception is approved by the CISO with documented residual-risk treatment and monitoring.
Information-sharing agreements, DATA Scheme controls and foreign/cross-border exchange
Entities manage the security risks associated with engaging with foreign partners.
Foreign partner integrations can introduce foreign interference, espionage, sovereignty and information-sharing risks that need explicit assessment and approval.
Conditional direct. Applies where NDIA integrates with foreign partners, foreign-hosted services or arrangements involving foreign access to NDIA data or systems.
Foreign partner and international integration controls

Integrations with foreign partners or foreign-hosted services must undergo security, sovereignty, legal and foreign interference risk assessment and be approved under NDIA and whole-of-government sharing arrangements before data exchange.
Classification, protective markings, metadata and caveat handling

The Australian Government Email Protective Marking Standard is applied to protect OFFICIAL and security classified information exchanged by email in and between Australian Government entities, including other authorised parties.
Email generated or routed by integration services can carry OFFICIAL or classified information and must use standard protective markings to support consistent handling and gateway control.
Conditional direct. Applies where integrations generate, route, ingest or exchange email messages, notifications or email-based data transfers.

Where integrations generate, route or exchange email notifications or messages, they must apply the Australian Government Email Protective Marking Standard to relevant protective markings and metadata.
Classification, protective markings, metadata and caveat handling

The Australian Government Recordkeeping Metadata Standard's 'Security Classification' property (and where relevant, the 'Security Caveat' property) is applied to protectively mark information on technology systems that store, process or communicate security classified information.
Classification and caveat metadata must survive system-to-system exchange so downstream systems can enforce handling, access and recordkeeping requirements.
Direct where integration data is security classified; good-practice baseline for sensitive NDIA data classifications and metadata mapping.
Data classification, caveats and metadata preservation

Integration payloads, records, messages and API metadata that store, process or communicate security classified information must preserve and transmit AGRkMS Security Classification and, where relevant, Security Caveat metadata.
Classification, protective markings, metadata and caveat handling
Apply the Australian Government Recordkeeping Metadata Standard's 'Rights' property where the entity wishes to categorise information content by the type of restrictions on access.
Rights metadata helps receiving systems understand restrictions on access, use and handling; integrations should not strip or ignore these attributes.
Conditional. Applies where NDIA needs to categorise information by access restrictions or downstream use limitations.
Access restriction metadata and rights handling

Where access restrictions need to be represented in integration data, integration designs must map and preserve AGRkMS Rights metadata or an approved equivalent to support downstream access control and handling.
Classification, protective markings, metadata and caveat handling

Access to security classified information or resources is only provided to people outside the entity with the appropriate security clearance (where required) and a need-to-know, and is transferred in accordance with the Minimum Protections and Handling Requirements.
Integration controls must enforce need-to-know, clearance and transfer protections before exposing classified or sensitive data to people or systems outside NDIA.
Direct for classified information and highly relevant to sensitive participant, provider and government information exchanged with external entities.
Access control and secure information transfer

Integration access must enforce need-to-know, clearance or eligibility where required, least privilege and data-transfer protections appropriate to the highest classification or sensitivity of the exchanged data.
Information-sharing agreements, DATA Scheme controls and foreign/cross-border exchange
The Memorandum of Understanding between the Commonwealth, States and Territories is applied when sharing information with state and territory government agencies.
State and territory integrations need to align with Commonwealth sharing arrangements when government information is exchanged across jurisdictions.
Conditional direct. Applies to NDIA integrations with state and territory government agencies and services.

Integrations with state or territory agencies must be supported by relevant Commonwealth-state-territory sharing arrangements and must reflect required security controls in interface agreements, onboarding evidence and operational procedures.
Information-sharing agreements, DATA Scheme controls and foreign/cross-border exchange
An agreement or arrangement is in place before security classified information or resources are disclosed or shared with a person or organisation outside of government.
External disclosure through an integration requires an agreement that defines recipients, purpose, controls, handling and accountabilities before data exchange occurs.
Direct for integrations sharing security classified information outside government; recommended for sensitive information shared with providers and partners.
Information sharing agreements and interface agreements

Before an integration shares security classified information outside government, NDIA must have an approved agreement or arrangement specifying purpose, authorised recipients, classification, handling, retention, security controls and incident obligations.
Information-sharing agreements, DATA Scheme controls and foreign/cross-border exchange
Provisions are met concerning the security of people, information and resources contained in international agreements and arrangements to which Australia is a party.
International information sharing obligations may impose additional controls on people, information and resources that must be reflected in integration designs.
Conditional. Applies to NDIA integrations involving international agreements or arrangements.
International integrations must comply with security provisions in applicable international agreements and arrangements, including people, information and resource protections.
Information-sharing agreements, DATA Scheme controls and foreign/cross-border exchange

Australian Government security classified information or resources shared with a foreign entity is protected by an explicit legislative provision, international agreement or international arrangement.
Australian Government classified data must not be shared with foreign entities through technical interfaces without a lawful authority or approved agreement.
Conditional. Applies where NDIA integrations could disclose Australian Government security classified information to foreign entities.
Foreign entity classified information sharing controls

NDIA must not share Australian Government security classified data with foreign entities through integrations unless an explicit legislative provision, international agreement or arrangement permits it and the approved controls are documented in the integration design.
Classification, protective markings, metadata and caveat handling

Australian Government security classified information or resources bearing the AUSTEO caveat is never shared with a person who is not an Australian citizen, even when an international agreement or arrangement is in place, unless an exemption is granted.
Caveat restrictions such as AUSTEO require technical controls to prevent unintended release through automated data exchange, routing or support access.
Conditional. Applies if NDIA integrations process, transmit or expose AUSTEO information or resources.

Integrations must prevent AUSTEO information or resources from being released to non-Australian citizens or unauthorised foreign systems unless an approved exemption is recorded and technically enforced.
Classification, protective markings, metadata and caveat handling
Australian Government security classified information or resources bearing the AGAO caveat is not shared with a person who is not an Australian citizen, except as specified.
AGAO caveated material requires recipient validation and release restrictions that must be enforced by integration access and routing controls.
Conditional. Applies if NDIA integrations process, transmit or expose AGAO-caveated information or resources.
Integrations must enforce AGAO caveat restrictions through access controls, routing rules and recipient validation so that non-Australian citizens receive access only where permitted.
Classification, protective markings, metadata and caveat handling

Where an international agreement or arrangement is in place, security classified foreign entity information or resources are safeguarded in accordance with the provisions set out in the agreement or arrangement.
Foreign-origin classified information may have handling and onward-sharing restrictions that must be preserved across NDIA integration flows.
Conditional. Applies where NDIA receives, processes or exchanges security classified foreign entity information or resources.

Where NDIA receives or exchanges foreign entity classified information through integrations, handling, storage, onward sharing and logging controls must follow the applicable agreement or arrangement.
Information-sharing agreements, DATA Scheme controls and foreign/cross-border exchange

Australian Government security classified information or resources shared with a foreign non-government stakeholder is protected by an explicit legislative provision, international agreement or international arrangement.
Foreign non-government stakeholder integrations present heightened disclosure and assurance risks and require lawful authority or an approved arrangement before any classified exchange.
Conditional. Applies to integrations with foreign non-government providers, partners, suppliers or stakeholders involving security classified information.

Integrations with foreign non-government stakeholders must not exchange Australian Government security classified information unless permitted by an explicit legislative provision, international agreement or arrangement and approved controls are implemented.
Security lifecycle, authorisation, asset register and change control
The Australian Signals Directorate's Information Security Manual cyber security principles are applied during all stages of the lifecycle of each system.
The ISM principles provide the baseline security posture for integration platforms, interfaces and supporting infrastructure across their lifecycle.
Direct. Applies to APIs, middleware, event platforms, message queues, file transfer, gateways, network connections, data pipelines and integration support tooling.
Secure integration lifecycle and ISM alignment

All integration platforms, APIs, middleware, gateways, data-transfer mechanisms and integration components must apply ASD ISM cyber security principles across design, build, test, deployment, operation, change and decommissioning.
Security lifecycle, authorisation, asset register and change control
The Australian Signals Directorate's Information Security Manual controls and cyber security guidelines are applied on a risk-based approach.
A risk-based ISM control approach is required because integration controls must vary by classification, exposure, partner risk and business criticality.
Direct. Applies to all new, changed and existing integrations proportionate to risk.
ISM control selection for integration patterns

Integration solution designs must select and implement ISM controls using a documented risk-based approach proportionate to data classification, threat exposure, connectivity, aggregation risk and business criticality.
Security lifecycle, authorisation, asset register and change control

The Authorising Officer authorises each technology system to operate based on the acceptance of the residual security risks associated with its operation before that system processes, stores or communicates government information or data.
Authorisation ensures residual risk is formally accepted before an integration processes, stores or communicates government information.
Direct. Applies before go-live for each integration system, platform, reusable service or material data flow.
Authorisation to operate and residual-risk acceptance

An integration must not process, store or communicate NDIA or government information until the relevant system or integration authorising officer has accepted residual risks and authorised it to operate.
Security lifecycle, authorisation, asset register and change control
Decisions to authorise (or reauthorise) a new technology system or make changes to an existing technology system are based on the ISM's risk-based approach to cyber security.
New integrations and major changes can change security exposure; authorisation and reauthorisation must follow the ISM risk-based approach.
Direct. Applies to new integrations, new partner connections, significant changes and control exceptions.
New integrations and material changes to existing integrations must use the ISM risk-based approach for security assessment, control selection, residual-risk acceptance and reauthorisation.
Security lifecycle, authorisation, asset register and change control
The technology system is authorised to the highest security classification of the information and data it will process, store or communicate.
Integrations can aggregate data or connect domains; authorisation must reflect the highest classification or sensitivity present in the flow.
Direct. Applies to integration platforms, API gateways, data hubs, event buses, managed file transfer services, databases and logs.

Integration platforms and interfaces must be authorised for the highest classification or sensitivity of the information they process, store or communicate, including aggregated data, metadata, logs and transformed data.
Security lifecycle, authorisation, asset register and change control

A register of the entity's authorised technology systems is developed, implemented and maintained, and includes the name and position of the Authorising Officer, system owner, date of authorisation, and any decisions to accept residual security risks.
An authorised systems register supports visibility of integration ownership, authorisation status, residual risks, classification and accountable officers.
Direct. Applies to integration platforms, services, gateways, connectors and external data exchanges that are part of NDIA's technology estate.
Authorised integrations register and service inventory

NDIA must maintain an authorised integrations register or ensure integration components are recorded in the authorised technology systems register, including system owner, authorising officer, date of authorisation, data classification and accepted residual risks.
Security lifecycle, authorisation, asset register and change control

Each technology system's suitability to be authorised to operate is reassessed when it undergoes significant functionality or architectural change, or where the system's security environment has changed considerably.
Changes to architecture, connectivity, data, threats or providers may invalidate previous authorisation and control assumptions.
Direct. Applies when integrations undergo significant functional, architectural, hosting, connectivity, partner, classification or control changes.
Material change assessment and reauthorisation triggers

Integration suitability and authorisation must be reassessed when functionality, architecture, data classification, partner connectivity, hosting, threat environment or security controls materially change.
Security lifecycle, authorisation, asset register and change control
The Australian Signals Directorate's temporary mitigations for legacy IT are applied to manage legacy information technology that cannot yet be replaced.
Legacy integration technology may not support required security controls; temporary mitigations and retirement planning are needed to manage residual risk.
Direct where legacy interfaces, protocols, middleware, certificates, network paths or partner services remain in use.

Legacy integration components that cannot be replaced must use ASD temporary mitigations and NDIA compensating controls, with time-bound remediation, enhanced monitoring and approved residual-risk acceptance.
Secure engineering controls, identity, secrets, encryption and monitoring
A Protective Domain Name System service or other security mechanisms is used to prevent connections to and from known malicious endpoints.
Internet-facing integrations are a common attack path; malicious endpoint blocking is a baseline protective control for integration traffic.
Direct. Applies to internet-connected APIs, gateways, partner endpoints, data transfer services, webhooks, middleware and cloud integration services.
Protective DNS and malicious endpoint controls
Internet-connected integration endpoints, gateways, middleware and platforms must use Protective DNS or equivalent security mechanisms to prevent connections to and from known malicious endpoints.
Cloud, hosting, gateway, regulated infrastructure and resilience
Cloud Service Providers that have completed an IRAP assessment against the latest version of ASD's ISM within the previous 24 months are used.
Cloud services used for integrations must have current independent assurance so NDIA can make risk-informed authorisation decisions.
Direct. Applies to cloud-hosted integration platforms, SaaS integration connectors, API management, gateways, managed file transfer and cloud middleware.
Cloud service assurance and IRAP requirements
Cloud services used for integrations must have a current IRAP assessment against the latest applicable ASD ISM release within the previous 24 months unless an approved exception is documented.
Cloud, hosting, gateway, regulated infrastructure and resilience
Entities consider IRAP assessment recommendations and findings, and implement on a risk-based approach.
IRAP findings must be assessed and treated; simply obtaining an assessment is insufficient for integration authorisation.
Direct. Applies to IRAP-assessed cloud, gateway, managed services and shared platforms used by NDIA integrations.
IRAP findings review and treatment tracking

Integration onboarding and authorisation must review IRAP assessment findings for cloud, gateway and managed services and must track risk-based treatments for findings affecting NDIA data, connectivity or security controls.
Cloud, hosting, gateway, regulated infrastructure and resilience

Security classified or systems of government significance information and data is securely hosted using a Cloud Service Provider and Data Centre Provider that has been certified against the Australian Government Hosting Certification Framework.
Hosting controls protect classified and high-value government data handled by integration platforms, data stores and processing services.
Conditional direct. Applies where integrations process, store or communicate security classified information or systems-of-government-significance data.
Hosting, cloud and data centre assurance

Integrations that process, store or communicate security classified or systems-of-government-significance data must use cloud and data centre providers certified under the Hosting Certification Framework where required.
Cloud, hosting, gateway, regulated infrastructure and resilience
The Data Centre Facilities Supplies Panel is used when procuring certified data centre space and services.
Certified data centre procurement is required where integration solutions rely on certified data centre space or services.
Conditional. Applies when NDIA procures certified data centre capacity, hosting or colocation for integration infrastructure.
When integration solutions require certified data centre space or services, procurement must use the Data Centre Facilities Supplies Panel or other mandated whole-of-government procurement channel.
Cloud, hosting, gateway, regulated infrastructure and resilience
Internet-connected technology systems, and the data they process, store or communicate, are protected by a gateway in accordance with the ISM and the Gateways Policy.
Internet-connected integrations require gateway controls to manage data flows across security domains and the internet boundary.
Direct. Applies to public APIs, internet-connected data exchanges, partner/provider connections, cloud ingress or egress paths and externally reachable services.
Gateway, SSE and network boundary controls

Internet-connected integrations and associated data flows must be protected by approved gateway or Security Service Edge capabilities designed and operated in accordance with the ISM and the Australian Government Gateway Security Standard.
Cloud, hosting, gateway, regulated infrastructure and resilience
Gateways or Secure Service Edges that have completed an IRAP assessment (or ASD assessment for TOP SECRET gateways) against the latest version of ASD's ISM within the previous 24 months are used.
Gateway and SSE services are critical integration control points and require current independent assessment to support trust and authorisation.
Direct. Applies to gateways, Secure Service Edge services, cloud security gateways, cross-domain gateways and managed gateway services used by integrations.

Gateway and Security Service Edge services used for integrations must have a current IRAP assessment, or ASD assessment for TOP SECRET gateways, against the latest ASD ISM within the previous 24 months.
Secure engineering controls, identity, secrets, encryption and monitoring
A vulnerability disclosure program and supporting processes and procedures are established to receive, verify, resolve and report on vulnerabilities disclosed by both internal and external sources.
Externally reachable integrations and APIs need a coordinated process to receive, verify, resolve and report vulnerabilities from internal and external sources.
Direct. Applies to public APIs, developer portals, integration platforms, webhooks, externally accessible services and provider-facing interfaces.

NDIA integration platforms, APIs and externally reachable services must be covered by a vulnerability disclosure process that receives, verifies, resolves and reports internally and externally disclosed vulnerabilities.
Security lifecycle, authorisation, asset register and change control

A Technology Asset Stocktake and Technology Security Risk Management Plan is created to identify and manage the entity's internet-facing systems or services to ensure continuous visibility and monitoring of the entity's resource and technology estate.
Continuous visibility of internet-facing integrations is required to manage exposure, monitoring and risk treatments across NDIA's technology estate.
Direct. Applies to internet-facing APIs, gateways, partner portals, webhooks, data exchange services and integration management planes.
Technology asset stocktake and exposure management

NDIA must identify internet-facing integrations, APIs, gateways and services in a technology asset stocktake and manage them through a technology security risk management plan to maintain visibility, monitoring and risk treatment.
Secure engineering controls, identity, secrets, encryption and monitoring
Approved post-quantum cryptographic encryption algorithms are used for newly procured cryptographic equipment and software in accordance with the ISM's guidelines for cryptography.
Integration confidentiality can depend on long-lived cryptography; new cryptographic products and software must be ready for post-quantum requirements.
Direct for newly procured integration cryptographic equipment and software; important for APIs, TLS termination, gateways, certificates, key management and data transfer.

Newly procured integration cryptographic equipment, libraries, certificates and software must support approved post-quantum cryptographic algorithms in line with ASD ISM cryptography guidance and NDIA cryptographic standards.
Cloud, hosting, gateway, regulated infrastructure and resilience

Digital Infrastructure that processes, stores or communicates Australian Government security classified information is protected by a Gateway or Security Service Edge in accordance with the Australian Government Gateway Security Standard.
Classified digital infrastructure used for integrations requires gateway or SSE protection aligned to the new Australian Government Gateway Security Standard.
Conditional direct. Applies where digital infrastructure supporting NDIA integrations processes, stores or communicates Australian Government security classified information.
Classified integration infrastructure and gateway protection

Digital infrastructure supporting integrations that process, store or communicate security classified information must be protected by gateway or Security Service Edge controls in accordance with the Australian Government Gateway Security Standard.
Secure engineering controls, identity, secrets, encryption and monitoring
Connect to the Australian Signals Directorate's Cyber Threat Intelligence Sharing platform.
Threat intelligence sharing improves detection and response for integration endpoints, APIs, gateways and exposed services.
Direct where NDIA security monitoring supports CTIS connectivity; relevant to cyber operations protecting integration services.
Threat intelligence sharing and integration monitoring

Integration security monitoring must support connection to ASD's Cyber Threat Intelligence Sharing platform where applicable, enabling timely ingestion and sharing of cyber threat intelligence for integration endpoints and platforms.
Cloud, hosting, gateway, regulated infrastructure and resilience
Declared Systems of Government Significance are protected in accordance with the Australian Government Systems of Government Significance Standard.
Declared Systems of Government Significance may impose additional obligations on connected integration services and data flows.
Conditional direct. Applies where an integration connects to, supports or exchanges data with a declared System of Government Significance.
Systems of Government Significance integration obligations

Integrations involving declared Systems of Government Significance must apply the Australian Government Systems of Government Significance Standard and document additional obligations in the integration architecture, security plan and operational controls.
Privacy, personal information, identifiers and sensitive health/identity data
Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles
Entities must manage personal information openly and transparently, with suitable privacy practices.
The ICT integration policy is a core privacy governance control for recurring data flows.
Privacy governance and privacy by design
Every integration involving personal information must complete privacy-by-design assessment before release.
Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles
Federal Register of Legislation; Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
Privacy, personal information, identifiers and sensitive health/identity data
Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles
Collect only reasonably necessary personal information and provide appropriate collection notices.
Silent or automated collection through APIs can scale privacy breaches quickly.
Data collection from participants, representatives, providers, partners and government sources.
Integrations must collect only approved fields and support clear privacy notices where collection is from an individual.
Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles
Federal Register of Legislation; Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
Privacy, personal information, identifiers and sensitive health/identity data
Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles
Use or disclose personal information only for the primary purpose or an authorised secondary purpose.
Reusable integrations create function-creep risk unless secondary use is controlled.
Internal reuse, partner sharing, provider access and government-to-government disclosures.
Data received through an integration must not be reused or forwarded for another purpose unless authorised and recorded.
Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles
Federal Register of Legislation; Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
Information-sharing agreements, DATA Scheme controls and foreign/cross-border exchange
Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles
Cross-border disclosure requires reasonable steps to ensure overseas recipients do not breach the APPs unless an exception applies.
Cloud, SaaS and offshore support can create overseas access even without intentional export.
Offshore hosting, support, subcontractors, global cloud regions or cross-border partner integrations.
Personal information must not be stored, routed or accessed offshore unless cross-border safeguards are approved.
Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles
Federal Register of Legislation; Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
Privacy, personal information, identifiers and sensitive health/identity data
Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles
Government identifiers must not be adopted, used or disclosed except where permitted; TFNs have extra rules.
Identifiers are tempting integration keys and matching fields but carry legal and linkage risks.
Medicare, Centrelink/CRN, TFN, healthcare identifiers, Digital ID and other government identifiers.
Government identifiers must only be used where lawful, necessary and approved; they must not become general-purpose keys.
Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles
Federal Register of Legislation; Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
Data governance, quality, matching and Indigenous data safeguards
Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles
Personal information must be accurate, accessible to individuals where required, and corrected where appropriate.
Integrated data errors can propagate into decisions, payments and participant communications.
Master data, participant details, provider details, plan data and transaction records.
Integrations must define source-of-truth rules and support correction, reconciliation and retrieval for access requests.
Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles
Federal Register of Legislation; Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
Privacy, personal information, identifiers and sensitive health/identity data
Privacy Act 1988 and Australian Privacy Principles
Entities must protect personal information and destroy or de-identify it when no longer required.
